subject: Pathology
vignette: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 8 hours after ingesting a large quantity of acetaminophen in a suicide attempt. He is initially well but then develops nausea, right upper quadrant pain, and markedly elevated serum transaminases. Biopsy shows centrilobular hepatocellular necrosis.
question: Which of the following best explains the mechanism of hepatic injury in this patient?

options.text: Immune complex deposition within hepatic sinusoids
Formation of a toxic metabolite via phase I metabolism causing free radical injury
Lysosomal enzyme release from infiltrating neutrophils
Saponification of hepatic fat by pancreatic lipase
Ischemic denaturation of enzymes with preserved cell outlines

explanation_correct: Acetaminophen overdose produces hepatotoxicity after metabolism of the drug by phase I reactions, which generates a reactive metabolite that causes free radical injury to hepatocytes, characteristically in the centrilobular zone. Free radicals damage cells through membrane lipid peroxidation, protein modification, and DNA breakage. This is the classic drug toxicity example of free radical injury, and the same category includes carbon tetrachloride, which is converted by cytochrome P-450 into the CCl3 free radical.

explanation_incorrect.A: Immune complex deposition in vessel walls is a type III hypersensitivity mechanism producing fibrinoid necrosis in vasculitis, and it does not explain centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis.
explanation_incorrect.B: Neutrophilic lysosomal enzymes digest tissue in liquefactive necrosis, which occurs in bacterial abscesses; the lesion here is toxic centrilobular hepatocyte death.
explanation_incorrect.C: Saponification by lipase is fat necrosis of adipose tissue in acute pancreatitis, and the liver injury described is hepatocellular rather than adipocyte necrosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Ischemia denatures enzymes and preserves cell outlines in coagulative necrosis, but this injury is toxic and metabolic, occurring through reactive metabolite generation.

educationalObjective: Acetaminophen overdose causes hepatotoxicity through phase I metabolism generating a reactive metabolite and free radical injury, classically producing centrilobular necrosis.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A premature infant born at 27 weeks of gestation is placed on supplemental oxygen. Several weeks later, ophthalmologic screening shows abnormal retinal vascularization. A second preterm infant in the same unit develops chronic lung disease with fibrotic changes. The neonatologist explains that both complications stem from the same fundamental mechanism.
question: Which of the following best describes this mechanism and the defenses against it?

options.text: Oxygen toxicity from free radicals, opposed by catalase, superoxide dismutase, and glutathione peroxidase
Amyloid deposition in the retina and lung, opposed by macrophages
Caseous necrosis from opportunistic infection, opposed by granuloma formation
Fat saponification in developing tissues, opposed by lipase inhibitors
Fibrinoid necrosis of retinal arteries, opposed by anticoagulation

explanation_correct: Supplemental oxygen generates free radicals, and oxygen toxicity in the preterm infant classically causes retinopathy of prematurity with abnormal vascularization and bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Free radicals injure cells through membrane lipid peroxidation, protein modification, and DNA breakage. They are eliminated by scavenging enzymes including catalase, superoxide dismutase, and glutathione peroxidase, as well as by spontaneous decay, antioxidants such as vitamins A, C, and E, and metal carrier proteins such as transferrin and ceruloplasmin.

explanation_incorrect.A: Amyloidosis is extracellular deposition of beta-pleated sheet protein, seen in conditions such as multiple myeloma and chronic inflammation, and is not the mechanism of oxygen-related injury in premature infants.
explanation_incorrect.B: Caseous necrosis reflects a granulomatous response to organisms such as tuberculosis and Histoplasma, whereas these complications result from oxidant injury rather than infection.
explanation_incorrect.C: Fat saponification is lipase-mediated necrosis of adipose tissue in acute pancreatitis or after trauma and has no role in retinopathy of prematurity or bronchopulmonary dysplasia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Fibrinoid necrosis from immune complexes or plasma protein leakage affects vessel walls in vasculitis and hypertensive emergency, not the developing retinal and pulmonary vasculature of a preterm infant.

educationalObjective: Oxygen toxicity from free radicals causes retinopathy of prematurity and bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and scavenging enzymes such as catalase, superoxide dismutase, and glutathione peroxidase protect against them.

subject: Pathology
vignette: A 48-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and bronze skin has markedly elevated hepatic iron stores on biopsy and a serum ferritin above 2000 ng/mL. His liver shows fibrosis and increased oxidative damage. Genetic testing confirms hereditary hemochromatosis.
question: Which of the following best explains how excess iron damages his hepatocytes?

options.text: Iron directly inhibits lysosomal enzymes, sparing the tissue
Iron blocks phase I drug metabolism, preventing toxin clearance
Iron participates in redox reactions generating free radicals, which peroxidize membrane lipids
Iron acts as an antioxidant, depleting intracellular calcium
Iron precipitates in mitochondria as psammoma bodies

explanation_correct: Transition metals such as iron and copper form free radicals through the Fenton reaction, and metal storage diseases including hemochromatosis and Wilson disease are classic examples of free radical injury. The radicals damage cells by membrane lipid peroxidation, protein modification, and DNA breakage. Normally iron is carried safely by transferrin, and ceruloplasmin handles copper, but in overload the unbound metal catalyzes oxidant chemistry and drives hepatic injury and fibrosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: Lysosomal rupture causing autolysis is a feature of irreversible cell injury, and iron does not protect tissue by inhibiting lysosomal enzymes.
explanation_incorrect.C: Phase I metabolism is a source of free radicals, for example in carbon tetrachloride conversion by cytochrome P-450, rather than a pathway that iron overload protects.
explanation_incorrect.D: Iron promotes rather than scavenges oxidant injury; antioxidants such as vitamins A, C, and E, and carrier proteins such as transferrin and ceruloplasmin, have the protective role.
explanation_incorrect.E: Psammoma bodies are concentrically laminated calcified spherules seen in tumors such as papillary thyroid and renal carcinoma, meningioma, and mesothelioma, not iron deposits in mitochondria.

educationalObjective: Iron and copper promote free radical formation through the Fenton reaction, so metal storage diseases such as hemochromatosis and Wilson disease illustrate oxidative injury.
